root_cause: Shared Python tool discovery did not resolve literal module lists through pure get_tools metadata, a private table builder and direct lookup/forwarding. Consequently shared flow rules did not enter the Proxmox handler. A plain global constructor was also resolved as a class callable before its actual instance initializer, hiding nested guard receiver identity.
correction: Reuse existing import resolution, ToolBinding, cached shared discovery, handler analysis and instance initialization. The bounded recognizer proves each module/provider/handler/name and unchanged lookup/arguments; no schema or negative-result safety inference. The normal coverage surface marks recognized dispatch only after actual binding; failed recognition retains unsupported coverage.
guard_boundary: Lazy global instances retain guard identity only if their included production import closure proves no instance/class mutation, escape, bound-method capture, unproved constructor-class attribute access including direct class calls, local protected import or reflective namespace access. Direct and global-alias receiver/class changes invalidate identity with an explicit unresolved diagnostic. Unknown runtime behavior is not a safe negative. No exclusions or accepted source contract are weakened.
limits: Only the explicit bounded builder/provider/forwarding form is supported; arbitrary computed registrations, dynamic names, package impersonation, duplicate names, mutated selectors and opaque aliases remain unsupported.
Complete module handler analysis retains conservative taint; names are not used to invent per-tool branch safety.

Source proofs cover the included production import closure. External runtime monkey patching, filesystem races, physical identity, successful exfiltration and arbitrary Python execution are not proved.

New current-source corpus support, positive detection and fixed/safe qualification remain unestablished pending separately approved regression. Original V80 Proxmox 0/2 detections and 0/4 supported negatives remain failures.
